questions.question: What is the time complexity of common array operations in Java?
questions.title: Array Operations Time Complexity | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: A Java array gives **O(1)** access by index and **O(1)** update, because elements sit in **contiguous memory** and the address is computed arithmetically. But **search** is **O(n)** (scan), and **insert/delete in the middle** is **O(n)** because everything after the spot must shift. Arrays are **fixed-size**; growing one (as `ArrayList` does) is amortized O(1) but O(n) on the resize copy.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know which array operations are cheap (index access) versus expensive (insert/delete/search) and why
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming insertion or search in an array is O(1) like index access, or confusing array with ArrayList growth
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Tie O(1) access to contiguous memory + base-address arithmetic, and explain ArrayList's amortized O(1) resize

sections.title: Array Operation Costs at a Glance
sections.content:
An **array** stores elements in **contiguous memory**, so the address of index `i` is `base + i * elementSize`. That single multiply-add is why **random access** and **update by index** are **O(1)** - the CPU jumps straight to the slot.

The costs people get wrong are the others. **Searching** for a value is **O(n)** (you may scan everything). **Inserting or deleting in the middle** is **O(n)** because every later element must shift one position. Arrays are **fixed-size** in Java; `ArrayList` simulates growth by allocating a bigger backing array and copying - O(n) on the resize, but **amortized O(1)** per `add` because doubling makes resizes rare.

sections.title: Array Costs at a Glance
sections.content:
emerald|Cheap O(1)|~direct address math|access a i|update a i = x|base + i * size
rose|Expensive O(n)|~must touch many|search unsorted|middle insert/delete|shift everything after
amber|ArrayList growth|~resize + copy|end add amortized O(1)|doubling backing array|rare full copies
blue|Fixed size|~plain arrays|cannot grow in place|sort enables O(log n) search|choose structure by need

sections.title: Big-O of Common Array Operations
sections.content:
| Operation | Complexity | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Access `a[i]` | **O(1)** | base + i * size address math |
| Update `a[i] = x` | **O(1)** | direct slot write |
| Search by value | **O(n)** | linear scan (unsorted) |
| Insert at end (`ArrayList`) | **O(1)** amortized | occasional resize copy |
| Insert/delete in middle | **O(n)** | shift all later elements |
| Resize (grow) | **O(n)** | allocate + copy backing array |

sections.title: Cheap vs Expensive in Code
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **'Insertion is O(1)'**: only at the end of an `ArrayList` (amortized); middle insertion is O(n) due to shifting.
- **'Search is fast'**: unsorted search is O(n); only a **sorted** array enables O(log n) binary search.
- **Array vs ArrayList**: plain arrays are fixed-size; resizing is something `ArrayList` does, not arrays themselves.
- **Ignoring the resize cost**: `ArrayList.add` is amortized O(1), but a single resize copies all n elements.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Access/update by index: O(1)** thanks to contiguous memory.
- **Search: O(n)** unsorted, **O(log n)** sorted (binary search).
- **Middle insert/delete: O(n)** - elements shift.
- **ArrayList end-add: amortized O(1)**, O(n) on resize.
- Arrays are **fixed-size**; growth means allocate + copy.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: The key thing about arrays is that the cost depends entirely on which operation you mean. Accessing or updating an element by its index is O of one, constant time, and the reason is that arrays live in contiguous memory. The address of element i is just the base address plus i times the element size, so the CPU computes that in one step and jumps straight there. Where freshers slip is assuming everything is that fast. Searching for a value, if the array isn't sorted, is O of n, because in the worst case you scan every element. Inserting or deleting in the middle is also O of n, because once you make or remove a slot, every element after it has to shift over by one position. The end case is special: adding to the end of an ArrayList is amortized O of one. It's usually constant, but every so often the backing array fills up, and the ArrayList allocates a bigger array, often double the size, and copies everything over, which is O of n for that one operation. Because doubling makes those resizes rare, the average cost per add stays constant. One distinction I'd draw is between a plain Java array and an ArrayList. A plain array is fixed-size; you can't grow it. The growth behavior, the resize and copy, is something ArrayList does on top of an array. So in interviews I'm careful to say index access is O of one, but search and middle insertion are O of n, and only a sorted array unlocks O of log n binary search.

questions.question: How do you reverse a string in Java without using built-in reverse methods?
questions.title: Reverse String in Java | Fresher Interview Question
questions.direct_answer: Convert the string to a `char[]` and swap with **two pointers** - one at the start, one at the end - moving inward until they meet. This is **O(n)** time and **O(n)** space for the char array (or O(1) extra if you reverse the array in place). Strings are **immutable** in Java, so you build a new string from the reversed characters.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can reverse manually with two pointers and remember Java strings are immutable
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Trying to mutate the String directly (impossible - it's immutable) or only reversing half/over-swapping past the middle
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use the two-pointer swap, stop at the middle, and mention immutability forces a char[] or StringBuilder

sections.title: Reversing a String by Hand
sections.content:
Java `String` is **immutable**, so you can't flip characters in place on the `String` itself - you work on a mutable `char[]` (or a `StringBuilder`). The classic manual approach is the **two-pointer swap**: `i` starts at index 0, `j` at the last index, swap `chars[i]` and `chars[j]`, then move `i++` and `j--`. Stop when they meet in the middle.

This is **O(n)** time - each character is touched once - and the `char[]` is **O(n)** space. Reversing the array itself uses O(1) extra space beyond that. The middle stop is important: swapping all the way to the end would undo your own work.

sections.title: Two-Pointer Reverse
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[chars = s.toCharArray
i=0, j=n-1] --> B{i < j?} B -- no --> Z[new String chars] B -- yes --> C[swap chars i, chars j] C --> D[i++
j--] D --> B ```

sections.title: Manual Reverse with Dry Run
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Mutating the String**: `s.charAt(i) = x` doesn't compile - strings are immutable; use a `char[]`.
- **Swapping past the middle**: looping while `i <= j` (or to the end) re-swaps and un-reverses.
- **Concatenation in a loop**: building the reversed string with `result += c` is O(n^2); use a char array or StringBuilder.
- **Unicode**: surrogate pairs (emoji) need care - per-`char` reversal can split them.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Strings are **immutable** - reverse a `char[]` then build a new String.
- **Two pointers** swap from both ends inward; stop at the middle (`i < j`).
- **O(n)** time; O(1) extra space if you reverse the array in place.
- Avoid `+=` in a loop (O(n^2)); use `char[]` or `StringBuilder`.
- `StringBuilder.reverse()` is the one-line library alternative.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: The first thing I'd point out is that Java strings are immutable, so I can't just swap characters inside the string itself. I convert the string to a char array, which is mutable, do the work there, and build a new string at the end. The reversal itself is a clean two-pointer swap. I put one index at the start, i equals zero, and another at the end, j equals length minus one. I swap the characters at i and j, then move i forward and j backward, and I keep going while i is less than j. The moment they meet in the middle I stop. That middle stop matters: if I kept going all the way to the end, I'd swap every pair twice and end up with the original string again. This runs in O of n time because I touch each character exactly once, and the char array is O of n space. A common mistake is trying to mutate the string directly, which doesn't even compile. Another is building the reversed string by concatenating in a loop with plus equals, which is O of n squared because strings are immutable and each concatenation copies everything. If I just need it done in real code, I'd use new StringBuilder of s dot reverse dot toString, which is one line, but in an interview the expectation is usually that I show the two-pointer loop. One subtlety I'd mention if asked is that characters outside the basic range, like emoji, are stored as surrogate pairs, and a naive per-character reversal can split them, so true Unicode-safe reversal needs extra handling.

questions.question: How do you find duplicates in an array in Java?
questions.title: Find Duplicates in Array Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Use a **HashSet**: scan the array, and for each element try to `add` it - if `add` returns `false` (already present) you found a duplicate. This is **O(n)** time and **O(n)** space, beating the **O(n^2)** brute-force double loop. If the array is sorted (or you sort it), adjacent equal elements reveal duplicates in O(n) with O(1) extra space.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you reach for a HashSet to trade space for time instead of the O(n^2) nested loop
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Defaulting to nested loops (O(n^2)) or forgetting HashSet.add returns false on a duplicate
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: State the space-time tradeoff and offer the sort-based O(1)-space alternative

sections.title: Finding Duplicates: Trade Space for Time
sections.content:
The brute force is a **double loop** comparing every pair - **O(n^2)**. The interview-standard fix uses a **HashSet** as a memory of what you've seen. As you scan, you try to `add` each element; `HashSet.add` returns **`false`** when the value is already present, which is your duplicate signal. That's **O(n)** time and **O(n)** space.

If you can sort first (or the input is sorted), duplicates become **adjacent**, so a single pass comparing `a[i]` with `a[i-1]` finds them in **O(n)** time and **O(1)** extra space - at the cost of O(n log n) sorting and reordering the data.

sections.title: HashSet Duplicate Scan
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
    A[seen = HashSet] --> B{more elements?}
    B -- no --> Z[no duplicates]
    B -- yes --> C[x = next element]
    C --> D{seen.add x == false?}
    D -- yes --> E[x is a duplicate]
    D -- no --> B
```

sections.title: HashSet Approach with Dry Run
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Nested loops by default**: O(n^2) is fine to mention but you should offer the O(n) HashSet version.
- **Forgetting add()'s return**: `HashSet.add` returns a boolean; using it avoids a separate `contains` call.
- **Reporting duplicates multiple times**: a value appearing 3x triggers two 'false' returns - dedupe if you need each only once.
- **Sorting when order matters**: the O(1)-space sort approach reorders the input; don't use it if original order is needed.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **HashSet**: O(n) time, O(n) space - the standard answer.
- `HashSet.add` returns **false** on a duplicate - use it directly.
- **Sort + adjacent compare**: O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space, but reorders data.
- Brute-force double loop is **O(n^2)** - last resort.
- Choose based on whether you can spend memory or must preserve order.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: The naive way is a double loop that compares every element with every other element, which is O of n squared. I'd mention it but immediately offer something better. The standard approach uses a HashSet as a record of what I've already seen. I scan the array once, and for each element I try to add it to the set. The nice part is that HashSet's add method returns a boolean: true if the value was new, and false if it was already in the set. So the moment add returns false, I know I've hit a duplicate. That gives me O of n time and O of n space, because in the worst case the set holds every element. I'd explicitly call this a space-for-time tradeoff, because that's what the interviewer wants to hear. If memory is tight, there's an alternative: sort the array first, which makes any duplicates land next to each other, and then a single pass comparing each element with the previous one finds them using only constant extra space. The catch is that sorting is O of n log n and it reorders the data, so I wouldn't use it if the original order matters. One detail to watch is a value that appears three or more times: it'll trigger the duplicate signal more than once, so if I only want to report each duplicate a single time, I dedupe the output. So my default is the HashSet for O of n, and I keep the sort-based approach in my back pocket for when space is the constraint.

How does a HashSet handle collisions?

questions.question: What is the two-sum problem and how do you solve it efficiently?
questions.title: Two Sum Problem Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Two Sum**: find two indices whose values add up to a target. The brute force is **O(n^2)**. The optimal uses a **HashMap of value -> index**: for each number `x`, check if `target - x` is already in the map; if so you have the pair, otherwise store `x`. That's **O(n)** time and **O(n)** space in a single pass.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can convert the O(n^2) pair search into an O(n) hash-map lookup in one pass
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Storing all elements first then searching (two passes) or using the same element twice for the pair
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Do it in one pass - check for the complement before inserting the current value

sections.title: Two Sum: The Complement Trick
sections.content:
The **Two Sum** problem asks for two array indices whose values sum to a `target`. Brute force checks every pair - **O(n^2)**. The key insight is the **complement**: for each value `x`, the partner you need is exactly `target - x`. If you remember the values you've already seen in a **HashMap (value -> index)**, you can ask in **O(1)** whether the complement is there.

The clean version is **single-pass**: before inserting `x`, check whether `target - x` is already in the map. If yes, return both indices; if no, store `x` and move on. **O(n)** time, **O(n)** space, and you never use the same element twice because you check before inserting.

sections.title: One-Pass Complement Lookup
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[map = value to index] --> B{more elements?} B -- no --> Z[no pair found] B -- yes --> C[x = nums i
need = target - x] C --> D{map contains need?} D -- yes --> E[return map.get need, i] D -- no --> F[map.put x, i] F --> B ```

sections.title: Brute force - O(n^2)
One-pass HashMap - O(n)
Key Points
sections.content:
- Partner of `x` is the **complement** `target - x`.
- **HashMap value->index** turns the pair search into O(1) lookups.
- **One pass**: check for the complement *before* inserting the current value.
- **O(n)** time, **O(n)** space - beats the O(n^2) double loop.
- Checking before inserting prevents reusing the same element.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Two Sum asks me to find two indices in an array whose values add up to a target. The brute force is a double loop checking every pair, which is O of n squared. The insight that makes it fast is the complement. For any value x, the only number that completes the pair is target minus x. So instead of searching for that partner by scanning, I keep a HashMap that maps each value I've seen to its index, which lets me check for the complement in constant time. The clean version does it in a single pass. As I walk through the array, for the current value I compute what I need, which is target minus the current value, and I ask the map whether I've already seen that complement. If I have, I immediately return the stored index and the current index. If I haven't, I put the current value and its index into the map and keep going. That's O of n time and O of n space. A subtle but important detail is the order: I check for the complement before I insert the current value. That guarantees I never pair an element with itself, because the current element isn't in the map yet when I do the lookup. A common mistake is doing it in two passes, filling the whole map first and then searching, which works but isn't necessary and can accidentally match an element with itself if you're not careful with indices. So the headline is: complement plus a hash map gives you Two Sum in one linear pass.

questions.question: How do you check if two strings are anagrams of each other?
questions.title: Check Anagram Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Two strings are **anagrams** if they contain the same characters with the same counts. The cleanest check is a **frequency count**: use an `int[26]` (lowercase letters), `++` for the first string, `--` for the second, then verify every bucket is zero. That's **O(n)** time and **O(1)** space. Sorting both and comparing also works but is **O(n log n)**.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you pick the O(n) counting approach over the O(n log n) sort, and check length first
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting the early length check, or assuming only 26 letters when input may be Unicode
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use a fixed int[26] for O(1) space and mention a HashMap for arbitrary/Unicode character sets

sections.title: Anagram Check by Character Frequency
sections.content:
Two strings are **anagrams** when one is a rearrangement of the other - same multiset of characters. First, a quick win: if the **lengths differ**, they can't be anagrams, so return early.

The optimal check is **counting**. For lowercase English, use an `int[26]`: increment for each char in string A, decrement for each char in string B. If they're anagrams, every count ends at **zero**. This is **O(n)** time and **O(1)** space (the array size is fixed at 26). The alternative - **sort both strings and compare** - is simpler to write but **O(n log n)**. For arbitrary or Unicode input, swap the fixed array for a `HashMap<Character, Integer>`.

sections.title: Counting Anagram Check
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A{a.length == b.length?} -- no --> X[not anagrams] A -- yes --> B[count = int 26] B --> C[for each char:
count a++
count b--] C --> D{all counts == 0?} D -- yes --> Y[anagrams] D -- no --> X ```

sections.title: Frequency Count with Dry Run
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **No length check**: different lengths can never be anagrams - check first to save work.
- **Assuming 26 letters**: `int[26]` only works for lowercase a-z; use a `HashMap` for mixed case, digits, or Unicode.
- **Sorting unnecessarily**: sorting is O(n log n); counting is O(n).
- **Case/space sensitivity**: decide up front whether 'Listen'/'Silent' or spaces count as equal.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Anagram = **same characters, same counts**.
- **Length mismatch** -> instantly not anagrams.
- **int[26] count** (++/--): O(n) time, O(1) space.
- Sort-and-compare works but is **O(n log n)**.
- Use a **HashMap** for Unicode / arbitrary alphabets.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Two strings are anagrams if one is just a rearrangement of the other, meaning they have exactly the same characters with the same counts. The very first thing I check is the lengths: if they're different, they can't possibly be anagrams, so I return false right away. For the main check, I have two approaches. The simplest to write is to sort both strings and compare them, but that's O of n log n because of the sorting. The approach I prefer is counting frequencies, which is O of n. For lowercase English letters I use an integer array of size twenty-six. I walk through both strings together, incrementing the count for each character in the first string and decrementing for each character in the second. If the two strings are anagrams, every increment is cancelled by a matching decrement, so at the end every bucket is zero. If any bucket is non-zero, they're not anagrams. That's linear time, and the space is constant because the array is a fixed twenty-six slots regardless of input size. I map a character to its bucket by subtracting the character a, so a goes to zero, b to one, and so on. The main caveat I'd raise is the alphabet assumption. The int twenty-six trick only works for lowercase a to z. If the input can include uppercase, digits, or Unicode characters, I'd switch to a HashMap from character to count, which handles any character set at the cost of a bit more overhead. I'd also clarify up front whether case and spaces should matter.

questions.question: What is the two-pointer technique and when do you use it on arrays?
questions.title: Two Pointer Technique Arrays
questions.direct_answer: The **two-pointer technique** uses two indices that move toward each other (or in the same direction) to avoid a nested loop. On a **sorted array**, put one pointer at each end: if the pair sum is too small move `left` right, if too big move `right` left. It turns many **O(n^2)** pair problems into **O(n)** with **O(1)** space.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the precondition (often sorted) and can explain why moving a pointer is provably safe
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using two pointers on unsorted data for sum problems, or not justifying which pointer to move
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the monotonic reasoning: in a sorted array, moving left/right strictly increases/decreases the sum

sections.title: Two Pointers: Replace the Nested Loop
sections.content:
The **two-pointer technique** keeps two indices into the array and advances them based on a condition, replacing an O(n^2) double loop with a single O(n) sweep. The most common form works on a **sorted array** with a pointer at each end.

For a target-sum problem: compute `nums[left] + nums[right]`. If it's **too small**, the only way to grow the sum is to move `left` rightward (toward larger values). If it's **too large**, move `right` leftward. Because the array is sorted, each move provably eliminates a whole set of impossible pairs, so you never miss the answer. Other variants move both pointers the **same direction** (fast/slow) for in-place filtering.

sections.title: Opposite-End Two Pointers
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[left=0, right=n-1
array sorted] --> B{left < right?} B -- no --> Z[no pair] B -- yes --> C[sum = nums left + nums right] C --> D{sum vs target} D -- equal --> E[found pair] D -- sum < target --> F[left++
need bigger] D -- sum > target --> G[right--
need smaller] F --> B G --> B ```

sections.title: Pair Sum with Two Pointers (Dry Run)
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Unsorted input**: the opposite-end sum technique needs a **sorted** array; sort first or use a HashMap.
- **Wrong pointer move**: moving the wrong pointer can skip the answer - tie the move to the comparison.
- **Off-by-one / overlap**: use `left < right` so the two pointers never cross or point at the same element.
- **Forgetting duplicates**: for problems like 3Sum, skip equal values to avoid duplicate results.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Two pointers replace an **O(n^2)** loop with **O(n)** time, **O(1)** space.
- Opposite-end form needs a **sorted** array.
- Move `left++` when the sum is too small, `right--` when too big.
- Monotonic order is what makes each move safe.
- Same-direction (fast/slow) variant handles in-place filtering and cycle detection.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: The two-pointer technique uses two indices into an array that I move based on some condition, and the payoff is replacing a nested loop, which would be O of n squared, with a single linear pass. The most common form works on a sorted array, with one pointer at the start and one at the end. Say I'm looking for two numbers that add up to a target. I add the values at the two pointers. If the sum is too small, the only way to increase it is to move the left pointer to the right, toward larger values, because the array is sorted. If the sum is too big, I move the right pointer left, toward smaller values. If it matches the target, I've found my pair. The reason this is correct, and what I'd emphasize, is the monotonic reasoning. Because the array is sorted, when the sum is too small I know that pairing the current right value with anything smaller than the current left value is hopeless, so I can safely discard that left pointer position and never miss a valid pair. Each move eliminates a whole batch of impossible combinations. The big precondition is that the array has to be sorted for this sum version; on unsorted data I'd either sort first or use a hash map instead. There's also a same-direction variant, a slow and a fast pointer moving the same way, which I use for in-place tasks like removing duplicates or for cycle detection in a linked list. Either way, two pointers give me O of n time and constant extra space.

questions.question: How do you find the maximum subarray sum (Kadane's algorithm)?
questions.title: Kadane's Algorithm Maximum Subarray
questions.direct_answer: **Kadane's algorithm** finds the maximum-sum contiguous subarray in **O(n)** time, **O(1)** space. Walk the array keeping `currentSum`: at each element take `max(num, currentSum + num)` - either extend the running subarray or restart at the current number - and track the best sum seen. The restart is the key idea: a negative running sum can only hurt, so drop it.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know Kadane's restart rule and can handle the all-negatives edge case
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Initializing maxSum to 0 (breaks on all-negative arrays) or not understanding when to restart
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the restart as 'a negative prefix is dead weight' and initialize maxSum to the first element

sections.title: Kadane's Algorithm: Extend or Restart
sections.content:
**Kadane's algorithm** computes the maximum sum of a **contiguous subarray** in a single pass. The core decision at each element `num` is: do I **extend** the current subarray (`currentSum + num`) or **restart** a fresh subarray at `num`? You pick whichever is larger: `currentSum = max(num, currentSum + num)`.

The intuition: if `currentSum` ever goes **negative**, carrying it forward only drags down future sums, so you abandon it and start over. You keep a separate `maxSum` for the best value seen so far. **O(n)** time, **O(1)** space. The classic trap is the **all-negative** array: initialize `maxSum` to the first element (not 0), or you'd wrongly return 0.

sections.title: Kadane Decision Flow
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[cur = nums 0
best = nums 0] --> B{more elements?} B -- no --> Z[return best] B -- yes --> C[num = next] C --> D[cur = max num, cur + num] D --> E[best = max best, cur] E --> B ```

sections.title: Kadane's with Dry Run
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **maxSum = 0 start**: fails on all-negative arrays like `{-3,-1,-2}` (returns 0 instead of -1). Initialize to `nums[0]`.
- **Resetting to 0 instead of `num`**: restarting at 0 ignores the current element; restart at `num`.
- **Confusing with max product**: Kadane is for sums; max product needs to track min too (negatives flip signs).
- **Returning the subarray**: if asked for indices, track start/end when you restart and when you update best.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Decision per element: `cur = max(num, cur + num)` - **extend or restart**.
- A **negative running sum** is dropped - it can only reduce future sums.
- Track a separate **best** = `max(best, cur)`.
- **O(n)** time, **O(1)** space.
- Initialize both to `nums[0]` to handle **all-negative** inputs.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Kadane's algorithm finds the maximum-sum contiguous subarray in one linear pass with constant extra space. The whole thing hinges on one decision I make at each element: should I extend the subarray I'm currently building, or throw it away and start fresh at the current element? I express that as current sum equals the max of the current number alone, or the current number plus the running sum. The reasoning is that if my running sum has gone negative, it's dead weight. Adding a negative prefix to whatever comes next only makes things worse, so I abandon it and restart at the current element. Alongside the running sum, I keep a separate best variable that records the highest sum I've ever seen, updating it each step. At the end, best is my answer. It's O of n time and O of one space. The classic trap, and the thing I'm careful about, is the all-negative array. If I initialize my best to zero, then for an array like negative three, negative one, negative two, I'd wrongly return zero, as if I could pick an empty subarray. So I initialize both the running sum and the best to the first element of the array, which correctly returns negative one in that case. Another subtlety is that when I restart, I restart at the current number, not at zero, because the subarray has to be non-empty. If the interviewer also wants the actual subarray and not just the sum, I track the start index whenever I restart and the end index whenever I update the best.

seo.metaTitle: Kadane's Algorithm Java Maximum Subarray | Fresher Interview
seo.metaDescription: Kadane's algorithm explained for Java fresher interviews. Find maximum subarray sum in O(n) time.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 app implementing array search and basic linked list operations
speakable_v2.hook: The moment your running total goes negative, it's pure dead weight - Kadane just drops it and starts the subarray over.

beats.text: Kadane's algorithm finds the contiguous subarray with the largest sum in a single pass. It keeps two values: currentSum (the best sum ending at the current position) and maxSum (the best seen globally). At each element it asks: 'Am I better off extending what I have, or starting fresh here?'

Brute force checks every possible subarray — O(n²) or worse. Kadane's is O(n) because the extend-or-restart decision means we never need to go back. It's essentially the simplest form of dynamic programming.

items: Initialise: currentSum = arr[0], maxSum = arr[0]
For each element from index 1: currentSum = Math.max(arr[i], currentSum + arr[i])
Update: maxSum = Math.max(maxSum, currentSum)
Return maxSum after the loop

beats.text: Array [-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4]. Walking through: currentSum becomes 1 at index 1, drops to -2 but resets to 4 at index 3, climbs to 6 at index 7, ending with maxSum of 6 for the subarray [4, -1, 2, 1]. candidates miss: initialise to arr[0] not 0 — if all numbers are negative, the answer is the least negative element, not zero, and zero initialisation gives the wrong result.

items: Initialising currentSum and maxSum to 0 breaks all-negative arrays — always use arr[0].
Resetting currentSum to 0 instead of arr[i] when restarting is a common coding slip.

speakable_v2.cap: Extend or restart — that's Kadane's in one phrase. Get the initialisation right and you've got O(n) maximum subarray.
